sections.title: A mountain system still changing
sections.body: The Canadian Rockies rise as folded and faulted layers of sedimentary rock, later carved by ice and running water. Within the World Heritage property, Banff, Jasper, Kootenay and Yoho national parks sit alongside three British Columbia provincial parks. Their lakes and sharp ridges are spectacular, but the geology explains the scenery: retreating glaciers leave sediment, expose rock and alter the courses of streams. The region is not a fixed mountain postcard.

sections.title: When the mountains were a sea
sections.body: At the Burgess Shale fossil localities in Yoho and Kootenay, fine-grained rock preserves creatures from an ancient marine ecosystem, including fragile body parts that rarely survive fossilisation. That contrast is remarkable: a visitor standing high in the mountains can encounter evidence of a long-vanished seabed. The fossils changed how scientists study early animal life, and their protected status makes collecting or disturbing them inappropriate.

sections.title: People, parks and conservation
sections.body: These mountain valleys were not discovered when national parks were created. Indigenous peoples have much older connections to the landscapes, and park histories also include the consequences of restrictions on land use and access. Modern management has to consider wildlife corridors, roads, tourism and changing snow and ice conditions. Celebrating the mountains should not hide those decisions or imply that conservation happens without people.

sections.title: Look beyond the blue lake
sections.body: The familiar turquoise water owes much of its colour to fine particles of rock carried into glacial lakes. Follow the water upstream and a lake becomes part of a wider story about erosion, climate and the mountains' ongoing transformation. The parks offer a connection between natural beauty and scientific evidence, rather than simply a collection of famous viewpoints.

records.quickFact: Ancient marine fossils survive in rocks now lifted high into the Canadian Rockies.

records.focus: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works
records.hook: Chile: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works

sections.title: Industry in the driest desert
sections.body: Near Iquique in Chile's Atacama region, Humberstone and Santa Laura preserve the remains of saltpetre production settlements. Buildings, processing equipment and open streets speak to an industry built in one of the driest environments on Earth. Sodium nitrate was extracted and processed for markets far beyond South America, linking this remote landscape with agriculture and industrial commerce around the world.

sections.title: A working community
sections.body: Workers and families came from Chile, Peru and Bolivia. Company towns were more than factories with houses attached: they developed shops, public spaces, distinctive speech and shared cultural traditions. The term pampinos refers to communities shaped by life on the desert pampa. Industrial heritage here includes their organising and struggles for fair treatment, not only the machinery that generated wealth for owners.

sections.title: Desert geography and global demand
sections.body: The extreme dryness helped preserve abandoned structures but also made everyday living demanding. Water, fuel, food and transport required organisation over great distances. A railway network linked many works across the region, while shifts in industrial production eventually transformed the economic importance of the nitrate fields. Understanding the settlement means following both local desert conditions and distant demand.

sections.title: Reading the ruins carefully
sections.body: An empty theatre or workshop invites an easy story of a vanished golden age. A better interpretation asks who worked there, who benefited and how living standards varied. Conservation is difficult because the fragile buildings face weathering and damage. The site was removed from UNESCO's danger list in 2019, but continuing care is still necessary.

records.quickFact: Workers at the saltpetre works helped create a distinctive pampinos culture across national backgrounds.

records.hook: Costa Rica: Área de Conservación Guanacaste

sections.title: A route through ecosystems
sections.body: In north-western Costa Rica, the Área de Conservación Guanacaste connects Pacific coastal habitats, tropical dry forest and wetter upland or inland forests. That sequence matters because animals, seeds and water move across ecological boundaries. Rather than protecting one isolated patch of greenery, the conservation area links contrasting environments along a route from shore to mountains. Seasonal differences can make neighbouring habitats look surprisingly unlike each other.

sections.title: The forest that changes colour
sections.body: Tropical dry forest is not failed rainforest. Many trees drop leaves during the dry season to conserve water, and the landscape changes dramatically with rainfall. A forest that appears sparse at one time of year may support complex food webs and new growth after rain returns. Regeneration and restoration work have made Guanacaste influential in thinking about how damaged tropical habitats can recover over decades.

sections.title: Biodiversity beyond a species list
sections.body: The protected area shelters numerous insects, plants and vertebrates, including species with specialised relationships to seasonal conditions. Coastal and marine environments add another layer to the story. Protecting connections across these habitats can be as important as safeguarding one charismatic animal. The UNESCO listing recognises ecological processes as well as the abundance of life, so a useful visit involves noticing change, movement and adaptation.

sections.title: Conservation has a human history
sections.body: The land has been used and altered by people over generations, and modern protection depends on research, management and engagement with neighbouring communities. Tourism can bring attention and income but also needs planning. Guanacaste shows that restoring natural processes is active work, not simply drawing a line around wilderness and leaving everything alone.

records.quickFact: A connected protected area runs from Pacific coastal ecosystems towards wetter forests inland.

records.hook: Egypt: Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis

sections.title: Two sides of the Nile
sections.body: Ancient Thebes developed around the Nile near present-day Luxor. Monumental temples stand on the eastern bank, while tombs and funerary sites occupy the western side. The river divided and connected these spaces, serving as a route for people and materials and as a source of water in an otherwise arid landscape. The geography helps explain why the settlement became such a powerful religious and political centre.

sections.title: Architecture built over generations
sections.body: Karnak is not the work of one ruler or a single building campaign. Its courts, columns and sanctuaries were changed and enlarged under successive pharaohs, while Luxor Temple became another important ceremonial place. On the west bank, the Valley of the Kings and surrounding necropolises show a different side of the same civilisation: ideas about death, royal authority and the afterlife expressed through architecture and decoration.

sections.title: Reading power and labour
sections.body: Enormous monuments reveal technical skill and coordinated labour, but they should not be mistaken for the whole of ancient Egyptian life. Craftspeople, agricultural workers, administrators and priests all helped sustain the city. The surviving archaeological record offers uneven views of these groups. Interpretation is stronger when it asks whose names and work were recorded and whose experiences are harder to recover.

sections.title: A landscape that still needs care
sections.body: Ancient stonework survives in a living region with residents, farming and tourism. Environmental conditions and visitor pressure affect conservation, while excavation continues to refine understanding of the past. Thebes is not all of Egypt, but it provides a detailed way into the relationship between river ecology, belief and monumental construction.

records.quickFact: Thebes joins the temple complexes of the Nile's east bank with major royal burial landscapes on the west.

sections.title: Mountains and the monsoon
sections.body: The Western Ghats run along western India, with steep slopes that influence how moist air moves inland. Rainfall varies sharply with height and position, producing a patchwork of wetter forest, highland habitats and more seasonal landscapes. The mountains are older than the Himalayas and have their own complex geological history. Their importance is geographical as well as scenic: they help shape water supplies and regional climate.

sections.title: Life found in few other places
sections.body: The UNESCO property protects parts of a biodiversity hotspot with high levels of endemism, meaning some plants and animals occur nowhere else. Amphibians, reptiles and forest trees are especially revealing examples of long evolutionary histories and specialised habitats. The area also supports larger animals such as elephants and gaur. A conservation account should focus on whole ecosystems, not assume that a spectacular mammal represents everything.

sections.title: Many protected places, one landscape
sections.body: The World Heritage property is made up of separate components rather than one continuous national park. That creates difficult questions about corridors, surrounding land use and management across several Indian states. Forests and waterways do not behave as though they belong to separate administrative offices. Protection requires coordination while recognising that people live and work in and around these mountain landscapes.

sections.title: Why small changes matter
sections.body: Changes in rainfall, forest cover or land use can affect rivers and wildlife far beyond the immediate site. The Western Ghats provide a way to see how mountain ecology connects with farms, settlements and downstream environments. Looking at moss, frogs and tree cover may reveal as much about environmental change as looking at a dramatic summit.

records.quickFact: Many Western Ghats species are endemic, and the mountain chain has a major influence on monsoon conditions.

sections.title: A forest with a long memory
sections.body: Shirakami-Sanchi lies in the mountains of northern Honshu, near the Sea of Japan. Its protected core includes an unusually extensive, largely undisturbed stand of Siebold's beech. The trees and slopes provide a living example of the cool-temperate forests that once spread more widely across northern Japan. Here the celebrated landscape is not a temple or an alpine skyline but a complex natural forest that has changed comparatively little under direct human development.

sections.title: Water, snow and trees
sections.body: Heavy precipitation and seasonal snow help shape streams, soils and the forest's annual rhythm. Beech roots and leaf litter contribute to an intricate ground environment, while steep hills and ravines create differences in shade and moisture. Forests respond to storms, disease and succession over time. That is why the place matters to scientists studying natural ecological processes as well as to people who value quiet woodland.

sections.title: Animals of the northern woods
sections.body: The reserve supports Japanese black bear, Japanese serow, birds and many less conspicuous organisms. Wildlife sightings are uncertain, and the important thing is the functioning habitat rather than close encounters with animals. Because the property contains very little infrastructure, access to the core must be managed carefully. Viewing the trees from a permitted trail is different from treating the entire protected forest as an unrestricted park.

sections.title: Beyond Japan's city image
sections.body: Japanese culture and history cannot be reduced to Tokyo streets or famous shrines. Shirakami-Sanchi offers a contrasting view of the country's northern landscapes and conservation choices. It asks an interesting question: how do you preserve a largely undisturbed forest while allowing people to understand why it is worth protecting?

records.quickFact: Shirakami-Sanchi protects one of East Asia's largest remaining natural beech forests.

sections.title: A lake across dry country
sections.body: Lake Turkana stretches through an arid region of northern Kenya, along the East African Rift. Its enormous water surface contrasts with the surrounding volcanic and desert-like landscapes. The lake is unusually saline for a large African lake, yet its waters and islands sustain ecological communities. Faulting, lava and sediment help explain the form of the basin, while rainfall and inflowing rivers influence conditions over time.

sections.title: Fossils and earlier climates
sections.body: The Koobi Fora deposits east of the lake preserve fossils that are central to research into human evolution and ancient environments. Fossils do not tell the full story of an individual life, but their geological context can reveal how landscapes and species changed. Remains of animals and hominins in different sediment layers make the region an exceptional outdoor archive. It connects modern Kenya with a much longer history of life.

sections.title: Islands and bird routes
sections.body: The World Heritage property includes Sibiloi National Park and parks on Central and South Islands. Birds use the lake during migration, while the islands are important habitats for Nile crocodiles and other wildlife. Ecological conditions can change with water level and human activity. It is more accurate to think of Turkana as an interacting lake basin than as a scenic shoreline with a few protected animals.

sections.title: People and environmental pressure
sections.body: Communities around the lake have their own livelihoods and cultural histories, which cannot be explained by the fossil record alone. Drought, water pressures and conservation management complicate decisions across the region. UNESCO has listed the national parks as World Heritage in Danger since 2018; that designation concerns conservation threats, not a blanket judgement about the people who live nearby.

records.quickFact: Koobi Fora fossils record earlier environments and help researchers investigate human ancestry.

records.focus: Te Wāhipounamu – South West New Zealand
records.hook: New Zealand: Te Wāhipounamu – South West New Zealand

sections.title: Land shaped by ice and uplift
sections.body: Te Wāhipounamu covers an extensive part of the south-west of New Zealand's South Island. Glaciers, rivers and tectonic uplift have helped carve deep fiords, valleys, lakes and steep mountains. The Alpine Fault marks a major plate boundary, so this landscape is still geologically active. From wet coastal forest to snow-covered peaks, short distances contain sharp changes in climate and habitat.

sections.title: Forests with ancient connections
sections.body: Southern beech and podocarp forests shelter plants and animals whose evolutionary history reaches back towards the former Gondwana landmass. Isolation helped New Zealand develop unusual wildlife, including distinctive birds with few close equivalents elsewhere. The kea is an alpine parrot, while the takahē has required careful conservation. Introduced predators remain a major problem for native species in many parts of the country.

sections.title: Names, people and responsibilities
sections.body: The region has strong connections to Ngāi Tahu, and management of protected land is not simply a matter of keeping people out. Māori histories and rights must be treated as part of the place, alongside more recent conservation and tourism systems. Popular tracks and boat trips show only selected corners of a far larger environment. Visitors should distinguish the accessible tourist routes from protected or remote areas.

sections.title: Notice the vertical journey
sections.body: A map of the south-west reveals an unusual sequence from sea to permanent snow. Follow an imagined drop of water and it may pass through glacier ice, waterfalls, dark forest and the Tasman Sea. The World Heritage area makes geological timescales and ecological connections unusually visible within one protected region.

records.quickFact: Fiords, glaciers and temperate rainforest sit close together across a geologically active part of the South Island.

sections.title: A city built from earth
sections.body: Chan Chan, near Trujillo on Peru's northern coast, was the capital of the Chimú kingdom before Inca expansion. It is famous for its extensive adobe structures, which demonstrate how a major urban centre could be created using local earth materials. The layout includes large walled compounds and distinctive decorative surfaces. These remains invite questions about urban planning, political authority and the everyday lives hidden behind monumental walls.

sections.title: Water in a coastal desert
sections.body: The area lies in a dry coastal environment, where irrigation was essential for large settlements and agriculture. Chan Chan's infrastructure and surroundings show that city building depended on managing scarce water, not just erecting palace compounds. The Chimú world also drew on coastal resources and craft production. Archaeologists investigate how political organisation connected food supplies, workshops and wider territories.

sections.title: More than a palace plan
sections.body: UNESCO describes nine major citadel-like units, but their imposing boundaries should not define an entire culture. Specialists also study smaller structures and traces of industries and settlement outside the most famous compounds. The city's history forms part of Peru's longer pre-Inca past, which varied considerably by region. What survives today is a selective record, shaped by original construction and centuries of erosion.

sections.title: Fragile heritage
sections.body: Adobe walls are especially vulnerable to moisture, wind, changing weather and inappropriate visitor contact. Conserving them requires more than making ruins look impressive for photographs. Chan Chan reveals a major civilisation through an unusual urban fabric, while also showing why archaeology in a desert environment needs constant attention to preservation.

records.quickFact: Chan Chan's Chimú planners organised an enormous adobe city around large enclosed compounds.

records.hook: South Korea: Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats

sections.title: The coast that disappears twice a day
sections.body: Along parts of South Korea's Yellow Sea coast, the sea retreats to expose extensive tidal flats before covering them again. These getbol are not empty mud. Tides, sediment, freshwater and saltwater create a changing set of habitats, including estuarine and island-associated wetlands. Their exact form varies from one section of coast to another, which is why the protected property includes several separate locations.

sections.title: A stopover on a long migration
sections.body: Migratory shorebirds use the exposed flats to feed on animals living within the sediment. Their journeys connect Korean coasts with breeding and wintering areas across the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. A flat that looks nearly featureless from a distance may supply the food needed for birds to continue thousands of kilometres. Protecting the habitat therefore has effects beyond one country or shoreline.

sections.title: Work and protection together
sections.body: Tidal flats are also places where people have long harvested marine resources, and nearby communities depend on healthy coastal systems. Conservation has to consider livelihoods, pollution and the effects of changing coastlines. South Korea's protection framework includes wetland and marine protected areas, while the 2026 World Heritage extension reflects a broader network of ecosystems. Reclamation and other coastal development can permanently change the sediment and water flows that sustain them.

sections.title: What to look for
sections.body: Watch the tide line rather than expecting a single spectacular landmark. Tiny burrows, channels and feeding birds reveal why these wetlands matter. The most surprising feature may be how much biodiversity depends on a habitat that is underwater for part of every day.

records.quickFact: Getbol are productive tidal ecosystems that feed migratory birds crossing international boundaries.

sections.title: Monuments before cities
sections.body: Göbekli Tepe, near Şanlıurfa in south-eastern Türkiye, contains monumental stone enclosures built during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. Groups of hunter-gatherers erected and carved large T-shaped limestone pillars in a period when ways of living and obtaining food were changing. Some pillars depict animals and human-like forms. Their scale raises fascinating questions about cooperation, specialist skills and communal gatherings long before familiar urban civilisations emerged.

sections.title: Reading the carved stones
sections.body: Wild animals appear on several pillars, but it would be careless to claim that every image has a certain religious meaning. Archaeologists interpret the enclosures through evidence from architecture, tools and excavation. Ritual or communal uses are plausible, though new research continues to refine the picture. The important achievement is visible without inventing a complete belief system: people organised complex construction with the techniques available to them.

sections.title: Stone and landscape
sections.body: The monuments were cut from limestone associated with the surrounding plateau. Quarrying, transporting and shaping such material required planning and labour. The structures are part of Upper Mesopotamia, a region central to debates about early settled life and farming. Göbekli Tepe should not be reduced to a sensational claim about the world's first temple; the site is better understood alongside other archaeological discoveries in the wider region.

sections.title: Preserving unanswered questions
sections.body: A protective roof and controlled visitor routes help reduce damage to excavated remains. Work at the site continues, so conclusions may change as archaeologists uncover more evidence. For visitors, the most revealing detail is the contrast between huge carved pillars and the limited material record available to explain the people who made them.

records.quickFact: Some T-shaped pillars stand over five metres tall and bear carvings of wild animals.

sections.title: A garden within a city
sections.body: The Singapore Botanic Gardens sit amid dense urban development, yet their paths and tree collections carry a long history. Established in 1859, the gardens changed from a colonial-era recreational landscape into a place for scientific research, plant conservation and public use. The lawns, buildings and planted collections reflect those different roles. It is a useful way to examine how a city can manage valuable green space without pretending that the park is untouched wilderness.

sections.title: Rubber and regional change
sections.body: Research and propagation work at the gardens helped the development of commercial rubber cultivation across Southeast Asia. That scientific achievement was also bound up with colonial trade and plantation economies, which brought major environmental and social changes. The story is more complicated than celebrating a botanical discovery. Studying this place involves asking how plant science, land ownership, labour and international markets affected one another.

sections.title: Living collections
sections.body: The gardens support tropical plant collections and horticultural education, including a major focus on orchids. Different planted areas demonstrate design choices as well as botanical knowledge. Trees offer shade in Singapore's hot, humid climate, while cultivated beds allow visitors to compare forms and adaptations. A managed garden is not the same as natural rainforest, but it can still support learning about biodiversity and conservation.

sections.title: Science and everyday life
sections.body: The grounds remain a public space where residents exercise, relax and encounter the city's landscape history. Their World Heritage status recognises the continuity of a cultural and scientific institution, not simply a large number of rare plants. Notice how the older layout, research activities and modern recreation coexist in an increasingly built-up city.

records.quickFact: Research at Singapore Botanic Gardens helped spread plantation rubber cultivation across Southeast Asia.
